symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on leaf surfaces; yellowing foliage; dark, scabby, sunken lesions on mature fruit.
causes: Fungal pathogen overwintering in fallen leaves. Spores are released in wet spring weather and spread by wind and splashing rain.

fungicides.name: Captan
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days from green tip stage until harvest.

fungicides.name: Myclobutanil
fungicides.frequency: Apply at 10-14 day intervals under preventive regimes.

treatment: Apply protective fungicides like Captan or systemic DMI fungicides like Myclobutanil during wet periods. Keep orchard floor free of fallen leaf litter.
prevention: Prune trees to open canopy and increase sunlight penetration. Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn. Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars like Enterprise or Liberty.
reference_sources: Cornell Fruit Resources, USDA Agricultural Research Service

symptoms: Small, water-soaked lesions on leaves turning black/brown with yellow halos; dark scabby lesions on fruit surface.
causes: Bacterial pathogen Xanthomonas. Spread by splashing rain, overhead irrigation, and contaminated tools. Thrives in warm, humid conditions.

fungicides.name: Copper Hydroxide
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days during periods of high humidity.

fungicides.name: Streptomycin Sulfate
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 5-7 days during bloom periods to prevent initial infection.

treatment: Apply copper-based bactericides. Use organic bactericides like Serenade (Bacillus subtilis). Remove and destroy infected plant debris.
prevention: Rotate crops every 2-3 years. Use disease-free seeds and transplants. Avoid overhead irrigation. Maintain good airflow between plants.
reference_sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension, Purdue University Extension

symptoms: Reddish-brown circular spots on leaves; fruit shrivels into black, wrinkled, hard mummies containing pycnidia.
causes: Fungal pathogen overwintering in vine mummies and cankers. Spread by wind-blown spores and splashing rain in wet weather.

fungicides.name: Mancozeb
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days starting at bud break until bloom.

fungicides.name: Ziram
fungicides.frequency: Apply at 7-14 day intervals under high disease pressure.

treatment: Apply protectant fungicides like Mancozeb early in the season. Remove all mummified fruit from the vineyard during winter pruning.
prevention: Remove and destroy all mummified fruit. Prune vines for maximum canopy airflow. Keep the vineyard floor clean and free of crop residue.
reference_sources: Ohio State University Extension, Penn State Extension

symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surfaces; tube-like structures (aecia) on the leaf undersides containing spores.
causes: Fungus requiring both apple trees and red cedars to complete its life cycle. Spores travel by wind between host species.

fungicides.name: Myclobutanil
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days from pink bud stage through petal fall.

fungicides.name: Mancozeb
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days starting at green tip stage.

treatment: Spray systemic DMI fungicides like Myclobutanil early in the season to disrupt rust spore cell wall synthesis.
prevention: Eradicate nearby red cedar trees within a 2-mile radius if possible. Plant resistant apple cultivars. Prune cedar galls before spring.
reference_sources: Virginia Tech Cooperative Extension, USDA Forest Service

disease: Cercospora leaf spot Gray leaf spot
symptoms: Rectangular, tan-to-gray lesions running parallel to leaf veins, eventually forming a grayish velvety sheen.
causes: Fungus overwintering in corn crop residue on the soil surface. Favored by high humidity and moderate temperatures.

fungicides.name: Pyraclostrobin
fungicides.frequency: Apply once at tassel stage or when lesions first appear on lower leaves.

fungicides.name: Propiconazole
fungicides.frequency: Apply at 7-14 day intervals if environmental conditions remain wet.

treatment: Apply strobilurin or triazole fungicides at the onset of disease. Manage crop debris via tillage.
prevention: Practice crop rotation for at least 1-2 years. Utilize conservation tillage to bury crop residues. Select tolerant hybrids.
reference_sources: Iowa State University Extension, Purdue Extension

symptoms: Cinnamon-brown, powdery, elongated pustules (uredinia) on both upper and lower leaf surfaces.
causes: Fungus spread by wind-borne spores originating in southern overwintering locations. Favored by cool temperatures and high dew.

fungicides.name: Azoxystrobin
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-14 days at the first sign of pustules.

fungicides.name: Pyraclostrobin
fungicides.frequency: Apply once or twice depending on field severity.

treatment: Apply strobilurin fungicides like Azoxystrobin to prevent cellular respiration of the rust spores.
prevention: Plant resistant crop hybrids. Manage canopy density to reduce leaf wetness and morning dew accumulation.
reference_sources: University of Illinois Extension, USDA Agricultural Research Service

symptoms: Target-like dark spots with concentric rings on older leaves; yellowing halos surrounding lesions; stem lesions.
causes: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. Survives in soil and plant debris. Favored by warm temperatures and high humidity or frequent rainfall.

fungicides.name: Chlorothalonil
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days as soon as weather conditions favor disease development.

fungicides.name: Copper Oxychloride
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days under organic management regimes.

treatment: Apply fungicides like Chlorothalonil or copper-based sprays. Use organic options like Neem oil or potassium bicarbonate. Prune lower leaves to improve airflow.
prevention: Keep foliage dry. Space plants properly. Mulch around the base. Practice crop rotation and remove garden debris after harvest.
reference_sources: North Carolina State University Extension, UC IPM

symptoms: Interveinal chlorosis and necrosis ('tiger stripe' leaves); small dark spots with purple halos on fruit; wood rotting/staining.
causes: Complex of wood-infecting fungal pathogens. Enter through pruning wounds during rain events.

fungicides.name: Thiophanate-methyl
fungicides.frequency: Spray immediately after pruning to protect open cuts.

fungicides.name: Myclobutanil
fungicides.frequency: Foliar/wound application during dormant pruning phases.

treatment: Protect pruning wounds with Thiophanate-methyl wound sealant. Prune out dead vines and replace with healthy plants.
prevention: Sanitize pruning tools with bleach or alcohol between vines. Avoid pruning during wet weather when spores are active.
reference_sources: UC IPM Guidelines for Grapevines, Oregon State University

symptoms: Blotchy mottled yellowing of leaves; small, asymmetric, bitter green fruit; twig dieback and stunted growth.
causes: Phloem-limited bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter. Transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid vector.

pesticides.name: Imidacloprid
pesticides.frequency: Apply as a soil drench once per season to control psyllids.

pesticides.name: Thiamethoxam
pesticides.frequency: Foliar spray every 14-21 days during flushing periods.

treatment: Incurable disease. Apply systemic neonicotinoid pesticides like Imidacloprid to suppress the citrus psyllid vector. Provide nutrient support.
prevention: Control Asian citrus psyllid populations using sticky traps. Remove and destroy infected trees to prevent farm transmission.
reference_sources: USDA APHIS, University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

symptoms: Large, irregular, water-soaked patches on leaves that quickly turn brown and papery. White fuzzy growth on the underside of leaves in humid weather. Dark brown lesions on stems.
causes: Caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Can destroy entire crops rapidly. Spread by wind-borne spores.

fungicides.name: Metalaxyl
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 10-14 days as a preventative or early curative spray.

fungicides.name: Cymoxanil
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days under high humidity conditions.

treatment: Immediate application of specialized systemic fungicides like Metalaxyl or Cymoxanil. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
prevention: Plant resistant varieties. Avoid planting near potatoes (which share the disease). Ensure good drainage. Monitor weather for cool and wet conditions.
reference_sources: Cornell University Vegetable Pathology, USDA Agricultural Research Service

symptoms: Pale green or yellowish spots on the upper surface of older leaves. Olive-green to brown velvety growth on the leaf underside. Leaves eventually turn brown and wither.
causes: Caused by the fungus Passalora fulva. Primarily occurs in greenhouses with high humidity (above 85%) and poor ventilation.

fungicides.name: Chlorothalonil
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days at first sign of symptoms.

fungicides.name: Copper Hydroxide
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days in organic systems.

treatment: Improve greenhouse ventilation. Use fungicides if infestation is severe. Organic treatments include copper-based sprays.
prevention: Reduce humidity. Prune for better airflow. Use resistant cultivars. Keep greenhouse temperatures above 60°F (15°C) at night.
reference_sources: Penn State Extension, Rutgers Cooperative Extension

symptoms: Small, dull brown or black spots on leaves, expanding to large necrotic patches and causing premature defoliation.
causes: Fungal pathogen Pseudocercospora vitis. Thrives in humid, warm grape canopy environments.

fungicides.name: Copper Oxychloride
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days starting post-bloom.

fungicides.name: Captan
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 10-14 days to protect new growth.

treatment: Apply contact copper or Captan fungicides to prevent spore germination. Prune lower foliage to increase air circulation.
prevention: Prune grape vines for high airflow, destroy all fallen leaf residue, and establish clean weed-free vineyard floors.
reference_sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension, University of Georgia Extension

symptoms: Necrotic brown edges on foliage; yellow halos separating dead and green tissue; scorched papery leaves.
causes: Can be bacterial (Xylella fastidiosa) or fungal (Diplocarpon earlianum). Spread by insect vectors or wet foliage.

pesticides.name: Imidacloprid
pesticides.frequency: Apply once as soil treatment to control vector insects (leafhoppers/sharpshooters).

treatment: If bacterial, manage vector insects with Imidacloprid. Remove and prune scorched branches to minimize spread.
prevention: Ensure proper irrigation to prevent environmental drought stress. Sanitize tools between cuts.
reference_sources: UC IPM guidelines, USDA Agricultural Research Service

symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped grayish-green lesions on leaves, progressing to complete blighting.
causes: Fungus overwintering in corn debris. Favored by wet, humid conditions and moderate temperatures.

fungicides.name: Pyraclostrobin
fungicides.frequency: Apply once at late vegetative stage or at first symptom onset.

fungicides.name: Propiconazole
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 10-14 days if wet weather continues.

treatment: Apply systemic fungicides like Pyraclostrobin or Propiconazole to protect upper leaf canopy.
prevention: Rotate crops with non-grass species, carry out deep tillage to bury crop debris, and plant resistant hybrids.
reference_sources: Iowa State Extension, Purdue Extension

symptoms: White, powdery, cobweb-like fungal patches on leaves, buds, and young stems; leaf curling and distortion.
causes: Fungal pathogens. Unlike most fungi, they do not require free water to germinate, thriving in high humidity and shade.

fungicides.name: Elemental Sulfur
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days starting at green tip stage.

fungicides.name: Myclobutanil
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 10-14 days to prevent leaf/fruit infections.

treatment: Spray sulfur or DMI fungicides like Myclobutanil. Organic options include Neem oil or potassium bicarbonate.
prevention: Ensure full sun exposure. Prune vines or tree canopies to improve airflow and reduce microclimatic humidity.
reference_sources: UC IPM Guidelines, Cornell University Fruit Resources

symptoms: Small, circular spots with gray centers and tiny black dots (pycnidia) in the middle; lower foliage turns yellow and falls off.
causes: Caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. Spreads by splashing water and contaminated tools. Can survive on weeds and crop debris.

fungicides.name: Chlorothalonil
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days immediately following rainfall events.

fungicides.name: Copper Hydroxide
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days under organic conditions.

treatment: Apply fungicides containing copper or chlorothalonil. Remove affected leaves to slow the spread. Use organic biofungicides.
prevention: Avoid overhead watering. Rotate crops. Keep the garden free of weeds. Use mulch to prevent soil splashing.
reference_sources: University of Wisconsin Extension, UC IPM

symptoms: Fine pale-yellow stippling on upper leaf surfaces; dense silken webbing on leaf undersides; leaf bronzing.
causes: Tetranychus urticae, tiny arachnids. Thrive in hot, dry conditions. Can multiply rapidly.

pesticides.name: Abamectin
pesticides.frequency: Apply every 7-14 days as needed to control spider mite outbreaks.

pesticides.name: Bifenazate
pesticides.mode_of_action: Mitochondrial complex III electron transport inhibitor (IRAC 20B)
pesticides.frequency: Apply once per season to break the mite life cycle.

treatment: Blast mites off with water. Use miticides like Abamectin or Bifenazate. Introduce predatory mites like Phytoseiulus persimilis.
prevention: Keep plants well-hydrated. Avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroid insecticides that destroy predatory insects and mites.
reference_sources: UC IPM Guidelines, Florida Department of Agriculture

symptoms: Circular brown spots with concentric rings, giving a 'target' appearance. Spots are larger than those of Early Blight and may have a yellow halo.
causes: Caused by the fungus Corynespora cassiicola. Favored by high humidity and temperatures between 70-85°F (21-30°C).

fungicides.name: Azoxystrobin
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-14 days at the first appearance of target spots.

fungicides.name: Chlorothalonil
fungicides.frequency: Apply every 7-10 days.

treatment: Spray with fungicides such as azoxystrobin or chlorothalonil. Organic control includes Neem oil or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.
prevention: Improve airflow. Avoid excessively long periods of leaf wetness. Manage weeds that may host the fungus.
reference_sources: University of Florida Extension, Auburn University Extension

symptoms: Severe stunting of plant growth; leaves cup/curl upward and turn pale yellow at borders; high rate of blossom drop.
causes: Transmitted by silverleaf whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). The virus is not spread by seeds or mechanical means.

pesticides.name: Imidacloprid
pesticides.frequency: Apply as a soil application at planting or side-dress.

pesticides.name: Acetamiprid
pesticides.frequency: Apply foliar spray every 7-14 days to control whitefly populations.

treatment: Incurable viral disease. Immediately remove and destroy infected tomato plants. Treat the whitefly vectors with Imidacloprid.
prevention: Use physical insect-proof netting in seedling stages. Plant certified TYLCV resistant cultivars. Control hosts/weeds nearby.
reference_sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension, UC IPM guidelines

symptoms: Mottling and green-yellow mosaic patterns on leaves; blistered, fern-like leaf malformations; internal browning of fruit.
causes: Highly contagious tobamovirus spread mechanically through hands, tools, soil, and seeds. Highly stable outside host.
treatment: Incurable viral disease. Uproot and burn or bury infected plants immediately. Do not touch adjacent plants.
prevention: Sanitize tools using a 10% household bleach solution or milk. Plant certified virus-free seed. Wash hands with soap thoroughly.
reference_sources: UC IPM guidelines, Cornell Cooperative Extension

symptoms: Lush green leaves, strong stems, and steady growth. No visible spots, wilting, or pests.
causes: Balanced nutrients, proper watering, and good environmental conditions.
treatment: Continue regular maintenance. Provide balanced organic fertilizer (e.g., compost tea).
prevention: Monitor daily for early signs of trouble. Maintain soil health with organic matter. Use clean water.
reference_sources: Healthy plants are the best defense against diseases and pests.

symptoms: N/A
causes: Poor soil quality leads to weak plants that are more susceptible to disease.
treatment: Amend soil with organic compost, well-rotted manure, or green manure. Ensure proper pH (usually 6.0-7.0 for tomatoes).
prevention: Test soil every 2-3 years. Use mulch to maintain moisture and suppress weeds.
additional_tips: Good soil structure (loamy) allows for better drainage and root penetration.

symptoms: Wilting, leaf curl, or blossom end rot due to inconsistent moisture.
causes: Overwatering or underwatering; watering foliage instead of soil.
treatment: Water at the base of the plant early in the morning. Use drip irrigation or soaker hoses.
prevention: Maintain consistent moisture levels. Avoid overhead watering to prevent fungal spread.
additional_tips: Deep watering once or twice a week is better than light daily watering.

symptoms: Holes in leaves, sticky residue (honeydew), or visible insects.
causes: Aphids, whiteflies, beetles, and other common garden pests.
treatment: Use Neem oil, insecticidal soap, or hot pepper sprays. Introduce beneficial insects like ladybugs.
prevention: Encourage biodiversity. Use companion planting to deter pests. Remove heavily infested plants.
additional_tips: Interplant with marigolds or basil to naturally repel many common pests.

symptoms: N/A
causes: Lack of biodiversity can lead to increased pest pressure.
treatment: Plant Marigolds with tomatoes to deter nematodes. Basil improves tomato flavor and repels flies and mosquitoes.
prevention: Plan your garden layout to include beneficial neighbors. Avoid planting fennel near most other plants.
additional_tips: Carrots, onions, and leeks are great companions that help deter each other's pests.

symptoms: Yellowing of lower leaves (Nitrogen), purple tint on leaf undersides (Phosphorus), or brown scorched edges (Potassium).
causes: Leached soil or improper pH preventing nutrient uptake.
treatment: Apply balanced organic fertilizer. Use fish emulsion for Nitrogen, bone meal for Phosphorus, and kelp meal for Potassium.
prevention: Test soil annually. Maintain organic matter with compost.
additional_tips: Over-fertilizing can be as harmful as under-fertilizing, often leading to lush but weak growth susceptible to pests.

symptoms: Dense foliage trapping humidity, leading to fungal issues like Leaf Mold or Powdery Mildew.
causes: Overcrowding and lack of pruning.
treatment: Prune 'suckers' from tomato plants. Remove bottom leaves that touch the soil.
prevention: Space plants according to variety recommendations. Stake or cage plants early.
additional_tips: Always use clean, sharp shears for pruning to avoid wounding the plant unnecessarily.
